1. Overview

In a post-collapse world, libraries become the vital repositories of human knowledge. Libraries preserve technical manuals, medical references, agricultural guides, and the cultural heritage that defines civilization. A well-organized library system enables communities to access critical information rapidly, support education, and prevent the loss of essential knowledge.

This guide covers the core principles of library science adapted for offline communities: classification systems, preservation techniques, and management practices that can be maintained without electricity or digital infrastructure.

Purpose of This Guide

Learn to:

  • Organize large book collections using proven systems
  • Preserve materials for decades using simple techniques
  • Create searchable catalogs without computers
  • Manage lending systems that prevent loss and theft
  • Design library spaces for community learning
  • Preserve and transmit oral knowledge alongside written records

2. Why Libraries Matter in Post-Collapse Communities

Before digital systems, libraries were humanity's primary knowledge repositories. They served multiple critical functions that become even more important when infrastructure fails:

Knowledge Access During Crisis

When grid electricity disappears, online databases become inaccessible. Communities need instant access to medical references, food preservation techniques, construction methods, and mechanical repair manuals. A well-organized library ensures critical information is available when needed most.

Education and Youth Development

Young people growing up without formal schooling require access to educational materials. Libraries support self-education, apprenticeship programs, and skill transmission. Books provide consistent, high-quality learning resources independent of individual teachers' availability.

Cultural Continuity

Libraries preserve art, literature, history, and philosophy. These materials maintain cultural identity and prevent psychological collapse. Reading provides mental health benefits during crisis periods and connects communities to the broader human experience.

Technical Knowledge Preservation

Specialized knowledge—engineering, medicine, agriculture, metallurgy—requires comprehensive written documentation. Libraries prevent the loss of centuries of technological development and ensure advanced skills remain transmissible across generations.

The most valuable library materials are technical references (medical texts, engineering manuals, agricultural guides), followed by educational materials, then cultural works. Prioritize acquiring these categories during the transition period.

3. Dewey Decimal System (Simplified)

The Dewey Decimal System (DDC) is the most widely adopted library classification method worldwide. While the complete system contains thousands of subdivisions, this simplified version provides enough granularity for community libraries while remaining manageable by hand.

Basic Structure

The system divides all knowledge into 10 main classes (000-900), each subdivided into 10 divisions, each subdivided into 10 sections. A three-digit number identifies the subject; decimal places allow further specificity.

RangeCategoryExamples
000-099Computer Science, Information & General WorksBibliography, General Knowledge, Information Science
100-199Philosophy & PsychologyEthics, Logic, Psychology, Self-help
200-299Religion & MythologyReligious texts, Church history, Mythology
300-399Social SciencesGovernment, Law, Economics, Sociology, Education
400-499LanguageDictionaries, Grammar, Writing guides
500-599Science & MathematicsChemistry, Physics, Biology, Medicine, Geology
600-699Technology & Applied SciencesEngineering, Construction, Agriculture, Cooking
700-799Arts & RecreationArchitecture, Music, Painting, Photography, Sports
800-899LiteratureFiction, Poetry, Drama, Essays
900-999History, Geography & BiographyHistory, Geography, Travel, Biography

Call Numbers for Community Libraries

Simplified format: XXX (three-digit Dewey class) + Author Surname Abbreviation

621.3 ENG (Engineering book by someone with surname starting 'ENG') 796.33 GRA (Sports book by someone with surname starting 'GRA') 615.5 LAR (Medical reference by someone with surname starting 'LAR')

Critical Subjects for Survival Communities

  • 615 - Pharmacology & Medicine: Essential. Acquire medical reference texts, nursing guides, pharmaceutical information.
  • 621-629 - Applied Physics & Engineering: Critical. Mechanical repair, construction, water systems, power generation.
  • 631-639 - Agriculture & Animal Husbandry: Essential. Crop production, food preservation, veterinary care.
  • 641 - Food & Drink: Essential. Cooking, food preservation, nutrition, food safety.
  • 682-684 - Woodworking & Metalworking: High value. Smithing, carpentry, tool making.
  • 701-799 - Arts & Architecture: Important for structural knowledge and morale.
  • 398 - Folklore & Mythology: Preserve cultural knowledge and traditional practices.

Field Notes: Dewey Implementation

Most surviving libraries will use simplified three-digit Dewey. Don't try to apply complex subcategories unless you have specialized training or library science reference texts. The 600s (Technology) section will be your most accessed and should be organized with extra care. Consider creating a separate "Quick Reference" section with 615, 621, 631, and 641 materials for emergency access.

Don't arbitrarily create new classification numbers. Stick to standard Dewey—this ensures any trained librarian can navigate your system and makes knowledge transferable to other communities.

4. Library of Congress Classification (Basics)

The Library of Congress (LC) system uses letters and numbers to classify materials. While more complex than Dewey, it's particularly useful for large specialized collections and is widely used in academic and research libraries.

Main Classes

CodeCategoryApplications
RMedicineMedical texts, anatomy, nursing, pharmacology
TTechnologyEngineering, construction, manufacturing, utilities
SAgricultureFarming, forestry, animal husbandry, food science
QSciencePhysics, chemistry, biology, geology, mathematics
KLawLegal systems, regulations, governance
JPolitical ScienceGovernment, politics, public administration
HSocial SciencesEconomics, sociology, education, psychology
PLanguage & LiteratureDictionaries, fiction, poetry, drama
GGeography & AnthropologyMaps, travel guides, cultural studies
E-FHistory of AmericasHistorical texts, biographies, regional history

When to Use LC vs Dewey

Use Dewey for: Small to medium community libraries (under 5,000 books), mixed collections, ease of use by untrained staff.

Use LC for: Large collections (10,000+ books), specialized libraries (medical, technical), integration with existing research library systems.

For most survival communities, Dewey Decimal is simpler to implement and maintain. Only adopt LC if you're preserving a large institutional library or integrating with existing LC-classified collections.

5. Card Catalog Construction

Card catalogs enable users to search library collections without computers. A well-designed manual card system allows rapid searching by title, author, and subject. This section covers construction and maintenance of hand-maintained catalogs.

Card Types and Formats

Standard library cards measure 3" x 5" (76mm x 127mm). This size has become standard for two reasons: it's large enough for legible handwriting and small enough to minimize storage space. Obtain acid-free cards if possible.

Card TypePurposeOrganization
Author CardPrimary record entry by author surnameAlphabetical by last name, then first name
Title CardSearchable by book titleAlphabetical by first significant word (skip "A", "The", "An")
Subject CardSearchable by topic/subject matterAlphabetical by subject heading (standardized list)
Cross-reference CardIndicates related subjectsPoints to other card locations

Catalog Card Layout

Card Writing Standards

  • Handwriting: Use black ink pen (fountain pen with permanent ink works well). Write legibly in capital letters for call numbers, title case for titles.
  • Call Number: Top left, large enough to read quickly from several feet away.
  • Author: Top line after call number. Format: Lastname, Firstname, birth-death years if known.
  • Title: Complete title as it appears on title page. Underline or mark in red for emphasis.
  • Publication: Place of publication, publisher, year. City : Publisher, YYYY.
  • Subject Headings: Use controlled vocabulary (standardized list). Underline with red pen.
  • Notes: Include edition information, illustrations, maps, diagrams, special features.

Card File Organization

Maintain three separate card files: Author File, Title File, and Subject File. Each file is alphabetically sorted in wood or cardboard card drawers. Dividers mark alphabetical sections (A-B, C-D, etc.). This provides three search pathways for users.

Field Notes: Card Catalog Maintenance

Establish monthly maintenance routine: Check for damaged cards, verify call numbers match actual book locations, update circulation status. If you acquire a new book, write one author card, one title card, and 2-3 subject cards same day. Keep blank cards and ink pens with the catalog area. Assign this task to a dedicated person or small team—consistency matters.

If handwriting multiple copies of the same card, use carbon paper to create author and title cards simultaneously. This saves time and ensures consistency between card copies.

6. Book Repair & Preservation

Books are fragile. Improper handling and storage cause rapid deterioration. Systematic preservation extends book life from decades to centuries and prevents loss of knowledge.

Common Damage Types and Prevention

Damage TypeCausePreventionRepair
Spine BreakingForcing book fully open, droppingHandle gently, don't over-flex. Support open books.Cloth tape over spine on inside; rebind if severe
Water DamageFlooding, moisture, condensationStore in dry location (below 60% humidity). Use desiccants.Air dry flat (2-4 weeks). Press between newsprint to flatten.
Mold & MildewHigh humidity, poor ventilationMaintain 30-50% humidity. Allow air circulation. Remove moldy books.Brush dry, air in sunlight, treat with boric acid solution
Torn PagesRough handling, age-brittlenessHandle with clean hands. Support pages when reading.Japanese tissue repair: glue acid-free tissue patch behind tear
Loose BindingAge, heavy use, moistureAvoid bending, support spine during readingRebind or reinforce with book tape and cloth
Foxing (Stains)Iron oxidation in paper, mold sporesStore in stable humidity and temperature. Handle with clean hands.Cannot be reversed; prevent spread by maintaining dry conditions

Basic Repair Supplies

Maintain a book repair kit with these essentials:

  • Acid-free book tape: For reinforcing torn spines and page edges
  • Japanese tissue: Thin, strong paper for page repairs
  • PVA adhesive: pH-neutral glue (not white glue, which is acidic)
  • Bone folder: Smooth tool for creasing and folding
  • Book press or weights: Heavy objects for flattening pages
  • Acid-free cardboard: For backing and reinforcement
  • Cotton cloth: For reinforcement strips
  • Scalpel or craft knife: For precise cutting

Tear Repair Procedure

Materials needed: Japanese tissue, PVA glue, bone folder, heavy weight

  1. Clean area around tear with soft brush to remove dirt
  2. Cut Japanese tissue slightly larger than tear (1-2cm on all sides)
  3. Apply thin, even coat of PVA glue to repair tissue
  4. Place tissue over tear from inside of page (if possible)
  5. Use bone folder to smooth out air bubbles
  6. Gently close book and weight it down for 24 hours
  7. Check repair after drying; excess tissue can be trimmed

Spine Reinforcement

For books with deteriorating spines:

  1. Open book to inside cover
  2. Apply 2-3cm width book tape along entire length of spine (inside)
  3. Use bone folder to press tape firmly to prevent bubbles
  4. If external spine is damaged, reinforce from inside with cloth tape first
  5. Allow adhesive to set fully before circulation

Don't attempt major rebinding unless trained. Poor rebinding can cause more damage than the original problem. For severely damaged books, consult with experienced conservators or preserve as reference-only materials.

Create a "Repair Log" documenting what books have been repaired, the work done, and when. This prevents redundant work and tracks material condition over time.

7. Archival Storage (Temperature, Humidity, Acid-free)

Environmental conditions dramatically impact book longevity. Books stored in optimal conditions can last centuries; books in poor conditions deteriorate in decades. This section covers archival storage principles.

Ideal Storage Environment

FactorIdeal RangeAcceptable RangeConsequences of Poor Conditions
Temperature60-70°F (15-21°C)55-75°F (13-24°C)Fluctuations cause expansion/contraction; heat accelerates deterioration
Relative Humidity30-40%25-50%Too dry: embrittlement; Too wet: mold, warping, ink bleeding
Light ExposureDarkness<50 lux, no UVFading, photo-degradation of paper and inks
Air QualityDust-free, non-pollutedFiltered airDust deposits; Pollutants cause chemical deterioration

Storage Space Design

Ideal locations: Interior basement (below grade, naturally cool), interior closets (stable temperature), or specially constructed storage room.

Avoid: Attics (temperature/humidity extremes), basements prone to flooding, spaces near HVAC vents (air currents), exterior walls (temperature swings).

Shelving and Book Arrangement

  • Shelving material: Acid-free wood (maple, oak) or steel shelving. Avoid particle board (off-gasses chemicals).
  • Shelf arrangement: Store books upright when possible (prevents spine damage). Rare/valuable books may be stored flat or at slight angle.
  • Book placement: Don't pack shelves too tightly; allow air circulation. Leave 5-10cm space behind books on back wall.
  • Weight distribution: Place heavier books on lower shelves to prevent structural strain.
  • Support: Use bookends to prevent leaning and warping.

Acid-Free Storage Materials

Paper becomes brittle when exposed to acid. All materials in contact with books should be acid-free:

  • Shelving: Unfinished wood, not plywood or particle board
  • Boxes: Acid-free archival cardboard (not regular cardboard)
  • Wrapping: Acid-free tissue or muslin
  • Padding: Acid-free polyester batting or wool felt
  • Dividers: Acid-free cardboard or plastic
  • Adhesives: PVA (polyvinyl acetate), avoid rubber cement or traditional pastes

Field Notes: DIY Humidity Control

Ideal storage has stable humidity 30-40%. If space humidity fluctuates: Use passive desiccants (silica gel, calcium chloride) during humid months. Replace when saturated. Maintain air circulation with small fan. Monitor with inexpensive humidity meter ($5-10). In dry climates, reverse process: Add moisture with damp sponges in sealed containers (monitor carefully to prevent mold).

Pest and Mold Prevention

Pests: Silverfish, bookworms, and roaches consume paper. Prevention:

  • Maintain storage at 50°F or below (slows insect reproduction)
  • Keep humidity at 40% or below (unfavorable to pests)
  • Inspect new acquisitions for signs of infestation before shelving
  • Quarantine infested books separately
  • Use diatomaceous earth (food-grade) around storage area perimeter

Mold: Grows above 50% humidity. Prevention:

  • Maintain humidity 30-40%
  • Allow air circulation (don't block air vents)
  • Avoid storing books in damp basements without humidity control
  • Remove any books showing mold signs immediately to prevent spread

If mold is already present in stored books, isolate them immediately. Mold spores spread rapidly to adjacent materials. Treat moldy books outdoors with careful brushing and sunlight exposure before returning to storage.

8. Lending Systems & Accountability

Libraries serve communities through lending. A good lending system ensures books circulate while remaining traceable. This prevents loss and enables recovery of missing materials.

Circulation Recording Methods

Three practical options for tracking loaned books:

Method 1: Checkout Card System (Recommended for Small Libraries)

How it works:

  • Each book contains a pocket glued inside back cover
  • Pocket contains a checkout card with call number and title
  • When book is loaned, borrower's name and return date written on card
  • Card removed and filed by return date or borrower name
  • When book returned, card reshelved in book pocket

Method 2: Borrower Register (Best for Accountability)

How it works:

  • Maintain a ledger organized by borrower name
  • Record call number, title, checkout date, and return date for each loan
  • Page per borrower or several borrowers per page depending on volume
  • Book is loaned by referencing this register only (no books from the shelf go home without entry)
  • Return is noted in the same register entry
Borrower: Sarah Martinez
Date OutCall # | TitleDate Returned
1/15/YY635.9 GRE - Gardening for Survival1/29/YY
2/5/YY641 COO - Food Preservation Guide2/28/YY
3/12/YY615.5 LAR - Medical Emergency Handbook—

Method 3: Library Card + Shelf Marker

How it works:

  • Each borrower receives a library card with name and ID number
  • When book loaned, card is placed on shelf where book was
  • Card remains as "placeholder" until book returned
  • Return requires finding matching book in collection and removing card
  • Excellent for visual identification of missing items

Lending Policies

Establish clear lending rules to ensure accountability:

  • Loan Duration: 14 days typical (shorter for high-demand materials)
  • Renewals: Allow 1-2 renewals if no one else waiting
  • Late Returns: Grace period (3 days) before penalty notice
  • Restricted Materials: Reference books, rare items, or critical supplies checked out in-library only
  • Overdue Recovery: Personal reminder visit, then formal community notification
  • Damage/Loss: Borrower responsible for replacement cost or repair

Field Notes: Circulation Management

Weekly: Review all current loans, identify returns due in next 7 days. Monthly: Reconcile checkout cards or register against physical inventory. Quarterly: Full inventory of collection, check for missing items, update borrower records. Keep overdue notices brief and non-punitive—most delays are simple forgetfulness. Community cooperation matters more than enforcement.

Consider "community access libraries" where books can be borrowed with verbal agreement only—especially critical technical materials. Trust-based systems work well in small communities and prevent knowledge hoarding during crises.

9. Reference vs Circulating Collections

Different materials serve different purposes. Reference collections support in-library research; circulating collections enable home borrowing. Strategic separation prevents loss of critical materials.

Reference Collection (Non-Circulating)

Purpose: Materials consulted for specific information that must remain available for immediate access.

Typical materials:

  • Medical reference texts (anatomy, pharmacology, emergency treatment)
  • Technical manuals and engineering handbooks
  • Dictionaries, encyclopedias, atlases
  • Rare or unique books (single copy only)
  • Government records and legal documents
  • Maps and charts
  • Indexes and bibliographies

Circulating Collection (Borrowable)

Purpose: Materials individuals take home for extended reading or study.

Typical materials:

  • Novels, poetry, fiction
  • Educational texts (if multiple copies available)
  • Technical books with multiple copies
  • Practical guides (cooking, gardening, handicrafts)
  • History and biography
  • Children's and young adult literature

Collection Development Strategy

Acquisition priorities (in order):

  1. Medical Reference: Emergency treatment, anatomy, pharmacology, nursing
  2. Technical/Engineering: Construction, mechanical repair, metalworking, electrical basics
  3. Agricultural: Crop production, food preservation, animal husbandry
  4. Educational: Mathematics, science, language, history textbooks
  5. Cultural/Literacy: Literature, poetry, history, philosophy
  6. Skills/Trades: Carpentry, masonry, blacksmithing, textile production
Material TypeReference | CirculatingPriorityTypical Copies
Emergency Medical GuideReferenceCritical2-3 copies
Engineering HandbookReferenceCritical1-2 copies
Food PreservationBothEssential1 ref + 2-3 circulating
Agricultural GuidesBothEssential1 ref + 2 circulating
Mathematics TextbooksBothImportant1 ref + 3-5 circulating
Fiction/LiteratureCirculatingImportant1-2 copies each
History/BiographyCirculatingModerate1 copy each

Never allow critical reference materials to circulate. A single medical reference that doesn't return during a crisis could cost lives. Keep at least one copy of essential materials in-library at all times.

10. Community Reading Programs

Libraries serve cultural and educational functions beyond basic access. Community reading programs develop literacy, preserve culture, and sustain mental health during crisis.

Literacy Programs

Goal: Ensure all community members can read and write at functional level.

  • Children's programs: Story hours, learning-to-read programs, youth reading groups
  • Adult literacy: Basic reading instruction for adults who missed formal education
  • Language programs: Teaching minority languages, dialect education for cultural preservation
  • Technical reading: Helping people understand manuals, specifications, and technical documentation

Educational Support Programs

  • Study groups: Organized groups working through educational texts together
  • Apprenticeship support: Library provides reference materials for apprentices in trades
  • Research assistance: Librarian helps people find information for specific projects
  • Skill workshops: Regular classes on topics like basic medicine, food preservation, or engineering basics

Cultural Preservation Programs

  • Story hours: Community members share oral stories, traditions, and cultural knowledge
  • Poetry readings: Public readings of literary works preserve cultural traditions
  • Discussion groups: Community reading and discussion of important texts
  • Archive projects: Recording and preserving local history, family stories, traditional practices

Mental Health & Morale Programs

During crisis, libraries support psychological wellbeing:

  • Escape reading: Fiction and literature provide mental respite and stress relief
  • Quiet space: Library serves as peaceful refuge from chaos
  • Community gathering: Reading programs bring people together, reducing isolation
  • Cultural continuity: Access to cultural and spiritual texts maintains identity and hope

Make library a welcoming social space. Comfortable seating, good lighting, and regular community events make the library a gathering place that strengthens community bonds beyond its information function.

11. Core Principles of Institutional Library Management

Successful libraries operate on foundational principles that guide all decisions. These principles help communities navigate conflicts, resource constraints, and changing priorities.

Universal Access as Foundation

Libraries function as knowledge commons—resources belong to the community, not individuals. Universal access principles ensure:

  • No person denied library access based on ability to pay
  • Knowledge reaches all community members regardless of literacy level, age, or status
  • Vulnerable populations (elders, children, disabled persons) receive special accommodation
  • Library serves as neutral community space open to all regardless of beliefs or background

Preservation Priority Over Circulation

When resources are limited, preservation supersedes convenience. Critical materials that cannot be easily replaced must be protected:

  • Reference materials never leave library building
  • Single-copy technical references shelved in restricted section
  • Rare or irreplaceable materials may be viewed in-library only with librarian supervision
  • This creates tension with accessibility but prevents permanent knowledge loss

Transparency in Collection Development

Communities should understand how library materials are selected:

  • Publish acquisition guidelines publicly
  • Accept community suggestions for materials (even if not all can be acquired)
  • Explain why certain materials are restricted to reference-only
  • Maintain records of what was requested but not acquired, revisit periodically

Core Library Principle: A library serves its community best when it balances three sometimes-conflicting priorities: universal access to knowledge, preservation of irreplaceable materials, and efficient use of limited storage and staff resources. No single principle always wins—judgment and community input determine the balance.

Neutral Ground Governance

Libraries function best as politically and religiously neutral spaces:

  • Collections include diverse viewpoints on controversial topics
  • Discussions are moderated without censorship
  • Materials are not removed due to political pressure (except in cases of serious misinformation about medical/safety topics)
  • Library does not advocate for particular ideologies while serving all equally

12. Implementation Steps for Starting a Community Library

Establishing a library requires planning, resource gathering, and gradual build-up. This section provides a realistic implementation timeline for communities beginning from minimal resources.

Phase 0: Preparation (Weeks 1-4)

Assessment and Planning:

  1. Conduct community survey: What materials are most needed? Who would use the library?
  2. Identify potential librarian/library coordinator (1-2 people minimum)
  3. Scout suitable location: temperature-stable, weatherproof, adequate space (500+ sq ft ideal)
  4. Establish library committee (5-7 community members representing different constituencies)
  5. Draft basic policies: lending duration, borrowing limits, reference vs. circulating guidelines
  6. Budget planning: estimate costs for shelving, preservation supplies, initial book acquisition

Resources needed: Committee consensus, 1-2 trained librarians (even if part-time), suitable space, initial funding for shelving and supplies

Phase 1: Infrastructure Setup (Weeks 5-12)

Space Preparation:

  1. Create stable environment: insulate, ventilate, control humidity, install basic shelving
  2. Acquire preservation supplies: acid-free storage materials, repair kit, monitoring equipment
  3. Organize three card catalog files with dividers and blank cards
  4. Create simple checkout tracking system (Method 1, 2, or 3 from lending section)
  5. Establish procedures manual: written documentation of all processes

Materials Acquisition:

  1. Start with highest-priority materials: medical references, technical manuals, agricultural guides
  2. Aim for 500-1000 volumes in Phase 1 (achievable through donation drives + strategic purchases)
  3. Catalog acquired materials immediately (don't let pile up)
  4. Create backup shelf in secure location for critical duplicates

Community Communication:

  1. Announce library opening and community input opportunities
  2. Establish regular community hours (start with 10 hours/week minimum)
  3. Recruit volunteers for shelving, cataloging, and facility maintenance

Phase 2: Operational Growth (Months 4-12)

Refinement:

  1. Monitor actual usage patterns; adjust lending policies if needed
  2. Track what materials are most requested; use data to guide future acquisitions
  3. Train secondary librarians and volunteers in classification and preservation
  4. Document all procedures; create cross-training for continuity
  5. Establish monthly maintenance routine: catalog updates, inventory checks, preservation review

Program Development:

  1. Launch first reading group or discussion program
  2. Begin oral history interviews with community knowledge-holders
  3. Develop collection of how-to guides specific to local needs (agriculture, medicine, crafts)
  4. Create children's literacy program if community has young learners

Field Notes: Realistic Timeline

Most successful community libraries take 6-12 months to establish functional operations. Don't rush. It's better to have 800 well-organized, well-preserved books than 3,000 chaotic, deteriorating ones. Focus early energy on systems and preservation, not collection size. Collections grow naturally through community donations and acquisitions; systems and preservation standards must be established from the start.

Phase 3: Expansion (Year 2+)

  • Expand hours, add evening/weekend access if demand exists
  • Develop specialized collections (medical sub-section, technical reference, etc.)
  • Establish satellite lending stations in other community areas
  • Integrate library with education programs, apprenticeships, and formal learning
  • Begin archival preservation of local documents, genealogies, and oral history

13. Roles & Responsibilities in Library Operations

Successful libraries require clear role definitions and adequate staffing. This section outlines minimum team structure for libraries of different sizes.

Small Library (300-1000 books, serving 50-200 community members)

Librarian/Coordinator (1 person, part-time 15-20 hours/week):

  • Oversees all operations, trains volunteers
  • Manages acquisitions and catalog updates
  • Handles complex circulation problems and patron disputes
  • Maintains preservation standards and storage conditions
  • Develops and executes library programs

Volunteers (2-3 people, rotating shifts):

  • Staff circulation desk, monitor lending
  • Shelve returns, straighten collection
  • Assist patrons with finding materials
  • Basic preservation work under librarian direction

Medium Library (1000-5000 books, serving 200-1000 members)

Head Librarian (1 person, full-time):

  • Overall library management and strategic planning
  • Staff supervision and training
  • Collection development policy and major acquisitions
  • Community relations and program development

Assistant Librarian (1 person, part-time 20-30 hours/week):

  • Day-to-day circulation management
  • Catalog maintenance and updates
  • Preservation and conservation work
  • Patron assistance and reference services

Circulation Desk Staff (2-3 people, part-time, rotating shifts):

  • Checkout and return processing
  • Patron registration and record keeping
  • Collection maintenance (shelving, organization)
  • Basic preservation work

Specialized Roles (as needed):

  • Conservation expert (part-time): Major repair work, humidity monitoring, pest prevention
  • Oral historian (volunteer): Interviewing, transcription, archiving
  • Technical specialist (volunteer): Maintaining catalog database, if computerized

Large Library (5000+ books, serving 1000+ members)

Director (1 person, full-time):

  • Strategic planning, budget oversight, board relations
  • Staff management and hiring
  • Community partnerships and program development
  • Major policy decisions

Head of Collections (1 part-time):

  • Acquisitions, deaccessioning decisions
  • Cataloging standards and oversight
  • Collection assessment and development

Head of Services (1 part-time):

  • Program development and execution
  • Patron services and community engagement
  • Literacy and education initiatives

Preservation/Conservation Specialist (1 part-time):

  • Book repair and restoration
  • Environmental monitoring and storage management
  • Staff training on preservation techniques

Circulation and Reference Staff (4-6 people, mix of full and part-time):

  • Circulation desk operations
  • Reference and research assistance
  • Patron registration and record management

Support Staff (1-2 people):

  • Facility maintenance
  • Shelving and organization
  • Clerical tasks

Critical Staffing Principle: All procedures must be documented and at least 2 people must understand each critical function. Single-person knowledge creates vulnerability. If the only person who knows catalog procedures gets sick or leaves, the library becomes dysfunctional. Cross-train continuously.

Volunteer Recruitment: Establish volunteer training program covering basic preservation, circulation procedures, and patron assistance. Volunteers provide essential capacity for small/medium libraries. Create meaningful roles—don't ask volunteers to just shelve. Involve them in collection development, programs, and decision-making.

14. Record-Keeping Systems & Accountability

Detailed records enable libraries to track materials, monitor usage patterns, and maintain accountability. This section covers essential record types and maintenance.

Essential Records to Maintain

Acquisition Records:

  • Track every book acquired: title, author, call number, acquisition date, source (donation, purchase, trade), condition upon receipt
  • Maintain running inventory total and format breakdown (reference vs. circulating, by major Dewey sections)
  • Record major donations with donor name (useful for thank-you, community relations)
  • Create acquisition log with serial numbers for barcodes or unique identifying marks

Circulation Records:

  • Complete checkout/return history (checkout date, return date, borrower) for every item
  • Track borrower records: patron name, contact info, items currently on loan, borrowing history
  • Overdue tracking: items not returned by due date, follow-up attempts, eventual recovery or write-off
  • Loss tracking: items never returned, presumed lost or stolen

Preservation/Maintenance Records:

  • Repair log: what was repaired, date, work performed, cost if applicable
  • Storage condition log: monthly humidity/temperature readings, pest sightings, mold detected
  • Inspection reports: inventory counts, condition assessments, damage found
  • Deaccessioning records: books removed from collection, reason (too damaged, outdated, replaced), disposal method

Personnel Records:

  • Staff/volunteer roster with contact info, roles, training completed
  • Training records: what each person trained in, certification dates
  • Incident reports: patron disputes, facility problems, security issues
  • Performance evaluations (if formal staff): annual or biannual assessments

Financial Records:

  • Budget tracking: income (if any), planned vs. actual spending
  • Acquisition costs: track spending by category
  • Preservation supply inventory and replacement schedule
  • Grant or donation tracking (if applicable)

Sample Preservation Log Template

DATE: [Date of inspection]
SECTION: [Dewey range, e.g., 600s Technology]
TEMPERATURE: [Current temp, recorded]
HUMIDITY: [Current %, recorded]
PEST SIGNS: [None observed / Silverfish / Roaches / Other - describe location]
MOLD DETECTED: [Location, extent, action taken]
BOOKS NEEDING REPAIR: [Call numbers, damage description]
ENVIRONMENT NOTES: [Air circulation adequate? Water stains? Ventilation issues?]
ACTION ITEMS: [What needs attention before next inspection]
INSPECTOR: [Name, date]

Record-Keeping Benefits: Detailed records accomplish multiple goals: they enable tracking of lost/overdue materials, provide data for collection development decisions, establish patterns (seasonal usage, popular categories), document preservation work, and create institutional memory. Spend 15 minutes daily on record updates rather than waiting to do it all monthly—this keeps records current and prevents backlogs.

15. Scaling Libraries for Large Communities or Multi-Site Systems

As communities grow, single-library models may need to expand into multi-branch systems or specialized collections. This section covers scaling challenges and solutions.

Single Large Library vs. Multiple Branches

Advantages of Single Large Library:

  • Centralized management, clearer accountability
  • Easier to maintain preservation standards
  • Broader collection serves broader needs
  • One decision-making structure

Advantages of Multiple Smaller Branches:

  • Better geographic access (people don't travel far for materials)
  • Specialized branches (medical library, technical library, children's library)
  • Community ownership (each neighborhood has its library)
  • Resilience (if one branch damaged, others continue)
  • Distributed knowledge preservation (copies in multiple locations as backup)

Hybrid Approach (Recommended for Medium-Large Communities):

  • Main central library: Houses complete collections, reference materials, rare items, administrative center
  • Neighborhood branches: 300-500 books each, high-demand materials, community gathering spaces
  • Rotating collection system: Books moved between branches based on demand
  • Unified catalog: Card catalog duplicated or referenced across all branches
  • Centralized policy: Same lending rules, preservation standards across system

Managing Multi-Branch Systems

Unified Policies & Procedures:

  • All branches use same classification system (Dewey or LC)
  • Identical lending policies and fees
  • Standardized card catalog format
  • Joint training program for all staff
  • Regular coordination meetings (monthly minimum)

Material Distribution Strategy:

  • Central library holds: reference materials, rare books, specialized technical collection, archives
  • Branch libraries hold: popular materials, how-to guides, fiction, local/regional history
  • Rotating collection: High-demand items move between branches monthly
  • Duplicate high-demand: Keep 2-3 copies of popular materials in different branches

Backup and Resilience:

  • Create backup card catalogs in at least 2 locations
  • Duplicate critical reference materials (medical, technical) across branches
  • Maintain copies of all preservation supplies and repair materials
  • Regular inventory coordination: central index of what's in each branch

Network Resilience: In multi-branch systems, distribute critical knowledge across locations. This provides redundancy—if one branch is destroyed, knowledge isn't lost. A medical reference library branch destroyed by fire becomes tragedy rather than catastrophe if copies exist in central library and other branches.

Satellite Lending Stations

For communities with limited reading culture or accessibility barriers, create lightweight satellite lending stations:

  • Small collection (50-100 high-demand books) in high-traffic area (market, school, town center)
  • Simplified checkout system (verbal agreement or simple register entry)
  • Rotating collection from main library
  • Staffed by volunteer (2-4 hours weekly minimum)
  • Goal: Increase access to reading materials for housebound, elderly, or traveling community members

16. Conflict Resolution in Library Management

Even well-run libraries encounter conflicts: disputed return dates, disagreements over collection decisions, or patron behavior problems. Clear procedures enable fair resolution.

Common Library Conflicts

Overdue/Lost Items:

Dispute: Patron claims they returned book; library records show still checked out.

Resolution Process:

  1. Review circulation records: date loaned, due date, return date if recorded
  2. Physical search: Check returned-book area, shelves to see if reshelved without recording
  3. Honest conversation: If still unresolved, accept patron statement if they offer reasonable explanation
  4. Documentation: Note outcome and agreement in borrower record
  5. Prevention: Ensure all returns are recorded before item leaves checkout desk

Collection Disputes:

Dispute: Community member demands removal of book they consider offensive/wrong.

Resolution Process:

  1. Acknowledge concern: "I understand why this material concerns you"
  2. Explain principle: "Our library includes diverse viewpoints so community members can form own opinions"
  3. Offer alternatives: "If this book isn't useful, you're welcome to suggest additions"
  4. Document: Record the complaint in collection file for future reference
  5. No removal: Unless material is factually dangerous (like incorrect medical information), keep it

Field Notes: Handling Book Challenges

Most book complaints come from genuine concern, not bad faith. Listen respectfully. Explain library collection principles. Most complainants will accept "library includes many viewpoints" rather than automatic removal. Rarely, content is genuinely dangerous (instructions for creating weapons, medical information that contradicts best practices for serious conditions). Use judgment—these require case-by-case evaluation with library committee input.

Patron Behavior:

Dispute: Patron monopolizes table/computer, speaking loudly, preventing others from using space.

Resolution Process:

  1. Address privately if possible: "Library space needs to be shared; could you lower your voice?"
  2. Establish time limits: "You're welcome to use this table for 2 hours, then others get a turn"
  3. Offer alternatives: "We have quieter study room available if you need different environment"
  4. Escalate if needed: For severe disruption, ask patron to leave for day
  5. Document: Record incident, what was said, what was decided
  6. Follow-up: Check in with patron before next visit, discuss expectations

Access Disputes:

Dispute: Librarian restricts patron access to reference section; patron feels discriminated against.

Resolution Process:

  1. Clarify policy: "Reference materials don't circulate because we need them available for everyone"
  2. Offer accommodation: "You can use any reference material here in-library during library hours"
  3. Understand need: "What information do you need? I can help you find it"
  4. Appeal process: If patron feels treated unfairly, library committee reviews decision
  5. Document: Record concern and resolution

Fairness Principle: All patrons must be treated equally under stated policies. If one person gets special access to reference materials, others must too. Consistency prevents perception of favoritism or discrimination.

Formal Appeal Process

For major disputes (collection removal demands, access restrictions, policy violations), establish appeal:

  1. Initial Decision: Librarian makes decision, communicates reasoning
  2. Written Appeal: Person disagreeing submits appeal in writing to library committee
  3. Committee Review: Committee meets, hears both sides, makes recommendation
  4. Implementation: Appeal upheld or denied, decision communicated with explanation
  5. Documentation: Appeal and outcome recorded in library records

17. Adaptation & Reform Over Time

Libraries must evolve as communities change, new technologies emerge, and needs shift. This section covers how to adapt library systems while maintaining stability.

When to Adapt Systems

Collection Development Changes:

  • If certain materials unused for 2+ years, identify why (outdated? wrong reading level? no community need?)
  • If particular subjects consistently high-demand, expand those sections
  • Seasonal adjustments: More agricultural materials in spring/summer, more heating/preservation materials in fall/winter
  • Post-crisis acquisition: After emergency (flood, fire, food shortage), adjust collection to address revealed gaps

Policy Evolution:

  • Lending policies: If loans consistently late, extend period. If materials damaged frequently, shorten period for certain categories.
  • Checkout procedures: If checkouts bottleneck, simplify system. If losses increase, add verification steps.
  • Reference policies: If patrons frustrated by access restrictions, consider limited-circulation options for less critical reference materials

Preservation Improvements:

  • If mold problems persistent, invest in better humidity control
  • If certain books repeatedly damaged, consider moving to reference-only or deaccessioning
  • If storage space becomes constraint, implement systematic deaccessioning of obsolete materials

Program Adjustments:

  • If reading groups sparsely attended, try different times/topics
  • If literacy programs show results, expand or intensify
  • If particular community members miss library (due to mobility/schedule issues), develop special services

Continuous Improvement: Establish quarterly library committee meetings to review: usage statistics, circulation data, preservation incidents, staff feedback. Use this data to identify needed changes. Small adjustments each quarter prevent major problems.

Deaccessioning (Removing Materials from Collection)

Over time, libraries must remove some materials: damaged beyond repair, outdated, or no longer serving community. Deaccessioning requires careful decision-making to avoid losing valuable knowledge.

Reasons to Deaccession:

  • Condition: Book is water-damaged, moldy, or structurally unsound beyond economic repair
  • Obsolescence: Information outdated (like 30-year-old computer manual with no historical value)
  • Duplication: Multiple copies when only one needed
  • Irrelevance: Materials no longer match community needs or library focus
  • Space constraints: Limited storage forces choices about what to keep

Deaccessioning Process:

  1. Review: Evaluate book condition, usage, and relevance
  2. Attempt preservation: Before removing, explore repair options
  3. Consider redistribution: Offer to other libraries if still useful
  4. Document: Record in deaccessioning log with reason and date
  5. Dispose responsibly: Donate to schools or other organizations, compost paper, never just discard
  6. Update records: Remove from catalog, update circulation records

Preservation vs. Space: Never deaccession valuable technical or medical references just to save space. If space constrained, expand storage or create satellite collection before losing knowledge. Deaccession less critical materials first (duplicate fiction, outdated coffee table books).

18. Decision-Making Processes & Community Governance

Libraries serve public good best when managed with community input. This section covers governance structures that balance expert librarian judgment with democratic community participation.

Library Committee Structure

Recommended Composition:

  • Head Librarian: Operational expert, attends all meetings
  • Community representatives (3-4): From different neighborhoods/constituencies
  • Skills representatives: Someone with book repair expertise, someone with preservation knowledge, someone with record-keeping experience
  • Youth representative: Ensures young people's needs considered
  • Optional: Elder or knowledge-holder, technical specialist if applicable

Meeting Frequency & Agenda:

  • Monthly: Strategic planning, collection development decisions, policy issues
  • Quarterly: Major assessment—usage data, budget review, preservation status, program evaluation
  • Annual: Budget approval, major policy reviews, community input sessions, strategic planning for coming year

Collection Development Decision-Making

Who Decides What Gets Acquired:

  • Librarian proposes: Based on community needs, preservation capacity, budget
  • Committee prioritizes: Evaluates proposals against acquisition criteria
  • Community input: Regular public suggestion period (anyone can request materials)
  • Final decision: Librarian makes final acquisition call within committee-approved budget and priorities

Criteria for Acquisition Decisions:

  1. Community need: Does community have use for this material?
  2. Quality: Is this reliable, well-written content?
  3. Preservation feasibility: Can we store/preserve this adequately?
  4. Collection balance: Does this fill gap or duplicate existing material?
  5. Budget: Can we afford this without cutting other priorities?
  6. Durability: Will this material withstand 10+ years of use?

Controversial Content Decision Process

When community members object to material:

  1. Receive complaint: Record in writing—what material, what concerns
  2. Review material: Librarian reads/evaluates, assesses complaint
  3. Research comparable opinions: Check if other libraries/experts view material as problematic
  4. Committee discussion: At next meeting, committee reviews material and complaint
  5. Decision criteria:
    • Is material factually accurate? (Medical accuracy especially important)
    • Does it serve library mission?
    • Are there harms from inclusion vs. exclusion?
  6. Communication: Explain decision to complainant and community
  7. Document: Record complaint and outcome for future reference

Governance Principle: Decisions matter most when made transparently with input from multiple perspectives. A decision community understands—even if they disagree—maintains trust better than expert decision without explanation. Document reasoning publicly so future library managers understand why decisions were made.

19. Oral Knowledge Preservation

Libraries preserve written knowledge, but much human learning is oral tradition—stories, skills, songs, and practices passed verbally. Systematic preservation of oral knowledge complements written collections.

Types of Oral Knowledge Worth Preserving

  • Technical skills: Descriptions of traditional techniques, tool use, material properties
  • Medical knowledge: Herbal remedies, treatment techniques, diagnostic methods
  • Agricultural practices: Planting calendars, soil management, seasonal knowledge specific to local conditions
  • Cultural stories: History, mythology, folklore that defines community identity
  • Family histories: Genealogy, ancestral stories, personal survival accounts
  • Wisdom traditions: Philosophy, spiritual practices, ethical teachings

Documentation Methods

Method 1: Transcription

Record oral knowledge in written form:

  • Conduct recorded interviews or conversations
  • Transcribe to permanent written record (handwritten or typed)
  • Organize chronologically, thematically, or by speaker
  • Store in archival folders with preservation standards
  • Index for searchability and cross-referencing

Method 2: Apprenticeship Recording

Document skills through structured teaching documentation:

  • Master craftsperson documents their knowledge while teaching apprentice
  • Create step-by-step written guides with illustrations
  • Record variation in technique, materials, and local adaptations
  • Preserve unusual or valuable techniques before they're lost

Method 3: Systematic Interview Archive

Create formal oral history project:

  1. Identify knowledge-holders in community (elders, experienced craftspeople, traditional healers)
  2. Develop interview protocol with standardized questions
  3. Conduct taped or recorded interviews
  4. Transcribe and organize materials
  5. Index by subject, interviewee, and knowledge type
  6. Make available for reference and study

Interview Protocol Template

ORAL HISTORY INTERVIEW FORM Interviewee: [Name, age, background] Date: [Date of interview] Location: [Where recorded] Interviewer: [Who conducted] Knowledge area: [Medical/Agricultural/Craft/Cultural/Other] Opening questions: - How did you learn this knowledge? - Who taught you? How long did training take? - What resources or materials are essential? - How has this knowledge changed over your lifetime? Technical questions: [Specific to knowledge area - variations, mistakes to avoid, innovations] Context questions: - When/where is this knowledge typically used? - What seasons, conditions, or circumstances affect practice? - How does this knowledge connect to other skills? Transmission questions: - Who else knows this? Have you taught others? - What's at risk of being lost? - What advice would you give to someone learning this? Closing: - Is there anything else important we should record? - Can we contact you with follow-up questions?

Field Notes: Oral History Project

Start small: Interview 3-5 community elders on topics critical to your area (food preservation, traditional medicine, local agriculture). Transcribe within 1 week while memory is fresh. File copies in multiple locations as backup. This preserves irreplaceable knowledge while honoring community elders. Over time, build archive of 50-100 interviews covering critical knowledge domains.

Pair oral history documentation with apprenticeship. When a master teaches an apprentice while documented, knowledge is both preserved AND actively transmitted, ensuring practical competence alongside written record.

20. Common Mistakes in Library Management

Learning from others' failures accelerates your success. Here are frequent errors in community library management:

Classification Mistakes

  • Inconsistent systems: Starting with one classification system then switching midway. Commit to Dewey OR LC early.
  • Arbitrary modifications: Adding non-standard call numbers or inventing new categories. Stick to standard systems.
  • Over-specialization: Creating 50 subcategories when 20 would suffice. Simplicity aids usability.
  • No authority control: Subject headings vary wildly (same topic called different things on different cards). Use standardized subject lists.

Preservation Mistakes

  • Acid-contamination: Using regular cardboard, particle board shelving, or acid-containing materials. Costs years of book life.
  • Poor storage conditions: Ignoring humidity/temperature (most common). This is the single biggest cause of deterioration.
  • DIY rebinding disasters: Attempting major repair without training, often causing more damage than original problem.
  • Neglecting inspection: Not checking new acquisitions for mold, pests, or damage before shelving.

Circulation Mistakes

  • No accountability system: Lending books without recording who has them. Makes recovery of lost items impossible.
  • Unclear lending policies: No stated loan period, late fees, or damage responsibility. Creates disputes.
  • Reference books circulating: Allowing critical reference materials to leave the library, where they're lost or not returned.
  • Poor organization of checkouts: Checkout cards scattered, register disorganized, no way to find current loans.

Collection Development Mistakes

  • Acquiring wrong books: Too many coffee table books, not enough technical references. Prioritize critical knowledge.
  • No duplicate copies: Single copy of important book means only one person at a time can access it.
  • Neglecting local needs: Acquiring books on topics irrelevant to community while missing locally essential materials.
  • Ignoring condition: Accepting water-damaged, moldy, or heavily worn books that will deteriorate further.

Staffing Mistakes

  • No documentation: All procedures exist in one person's head; library collapses when they leave.
  • Insufficient training: Library staff unclear on classification, preservation, or policies, leading to inconsistent application.
  • Overwork: One person trying to do everything; library deteriorates from fatigue and overwhelm.
  • No succession planning: Not training younger people to eventually take over library management.

Community Engagement Mistakes

  • Library as resource hoarding: Restricting access or making borrowing difficult breeds resentment and reduces usage.
  • No community input: Not asking users what materials they need; library becomes disconnected from community interests.
  • Neglecting literacy programs: Assuming everyone can read; opportunity lost to improve community literacy.
  • Poor mental health of library: Unwelcoming space, poor lighting, uncomfortable seating discourages use.

The most common and costly mistake: Not maintaining proper storage conditions (temperature/humidity). This single factor causes more book deterioration than all other factors combined. Monitor this obsessively.

Document everything in writing. Create a Library Manual covering classification system, preservation procedures, circulation policies, and disaster response. This prevents knowledge loss and enables smooth transitions when someone leaves.
